source: Web research conducted 2026-08-06 for Rootstock design. Primary sources: ~20 Chief Delphi threads read in full via the Discourse JSON API (chiefdelphi.com/t/<id>.json — note: WebFetch gets HTTP 403 on chiefdelphi.com, curl/fetch with a browser UA works); docs.wpilib.org (2026 stable + 2027 "latest"); CTR Electronics changelog & Phoenix 6 docs; docs.advantagekit.org; docs.yagsl.com; GitHub (AdvantageKit, FrcCatalyst, 3061-lib, Robonauts-Everybot, maple-sim). LIMITATIONS I could not work around: reddit.com is blocked to Anthropic's crawler (no r/FRC data — every r/FRC claim below is absent, not verified); FRC Discord is not fetchable and no public summaries were found; the 118everybot.org software-philosophy quote surfaced only via search-engine snippet and I could NOT verify it on the source page or in the repo README.
summary: The single largest fact for a library being designed in Aug 2026 is that the 2026 season is a dead-end target: WPILib 2027 moves to SystemCore, `edu.wpi.first` → `org.wpilib`, Java 25, Commands v3 (coroutines + a built-in declarative state-machine API), and removes Shuffleboard/SmartDashboard/PathWeaver/RobotBuilder while adding first-party Telemetry and Tunable APIs — and "it will not be possible to have the same code target both the 2026 and 2027 libraries" (Peter Johnson, WPILib lead, https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/517572/14). Small-team pain is remarkably consistent across sources: swerve bring-up dominates the help forums (dozens of distinct 2026 "YAGSL <specific failure>" threads), programmers get no robot for the first 4+ weeks, the one or two students who understand the code graduate and take it with them (one team literally had its working code deleted on the way out: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/504585), and rookie programmers hit a wall not on control theory but on Java OOP + the periodic/callback model. The community's verdict on existing batteries-included stacks is bimodal and instructive: YASS (YAGSL/YAMS/YALL/YAMG) reports 500+ teams and 35/50 US states, AdvantageKit 600+ teams and 200+ on its swerve templates, yet the 2026 YASS feedback thread is a sustained critique of exactly the design choices a "Rootstock" would be tempted to make — a monolithic `SmartMotorController` that hides on-motor vs on-RIO loops, a wall of config knobs no CSA can bisect, and docs that drifted (including an AI-written feedforward error: "sin should be cos"). The clearest positive signal in the whole corpus is that **code generation beat runtime abstraction**: YAMGen (which deliberately does NOT use YAMS underneath) was called "the most useful part of the YASS stack… the codegen route is far more useful than YAMS, and comes with fewer footguns" by a working CSA, and CTRE shipped `corvus`, a JSON→mechanism-code CLI, plus Tuner X Swerve/Elevator/Arm/Flywheel generators. Debuggability, not feature count, is the currency: "debugging speed is incredibly important in FRC; a program where most teams give relatively little hands-on time to programmers. Every hour spent debugging is an hour you're not spending doing driver practice."
stack:
**2026 baseline (what teams actually ran):** WPILib 2026 (Java ~90% of teams per https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/509064), command-based v2, `edu.wpi.first` packages. Motor controllers: CTRE Phoenix 6 (Kraken X60/X44, TalonFX/TalonFXS, Minion) and REV (SPARK MAX/Flex, NEO). Sensors: CANcoder, Pigeon 2, Canandgyro, NavX (Studica), CANdi/CANrange. Swerve: SDS MK4/MK4i/MK4n/MK5i, REV MAXSwerve. Vision: PhotonVision, Limelight, QuestNav. Pathing: PathPlanner (2026 release was a no-major-change release explicitly holding off "for the 2027 switch to SystemCore" — https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/509227/10), Choreo, BLine. Dashboards: Elastic (bundled in WPILib since 2025; "used by 1235 different teams in matches" per usage reporting — https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/506888), AdvantageScope. Logging: AdvantageKit (600+ teams 2025), WPILib DataLog/Epilogue `@Logged`. Sim: WPILib sim + maple-sim (dyn4j physics, game-piece collisions; bundled into YAGSL). Third-party frameworks: YASS = YAGSL (swerve) + YAMS (mechanisms) + YALL (Limelight) + YAMGen (codegen); AdvantageKit template projects (KitBot, differential, Spark swerve, TalonFX(S) swerve, vision, skeleton); 3061-lib (HuskieRobotics — CTRE+SDS only "out of the box", multi-robot configs, AdvantageKit-based); FrcCatalyst (Phoenix-6-only builder library, MIT, 11 GitHub stars, 78 JUnit tests, effectively one student maintainer); Team100 lib; Ylib (3211). Official low-resource starting points: FRC KitBot (2026 Java guide ships two projects showing different Command styles) and Robonauts 118 Everybot ("specifically targeted towards under-resourced and under-mentored teams", ~$1500 + KOP — https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/510331).

**2027 target (what Rootstock must actually ship against):** SystemCore (Raspberry Pi CM5 + RP2350 for reconfigurable IO, quad-core Cortex-A76, onboard IMU, multiple CAN buses, Smart IO, Expansion Hub — https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/software/systemcore-info/systemcore-introduction.html). WPILib 2027: Java 25 / C++23, `org.wpilib` packages, `wpi::` namespaces, NetworkTables v3 support removed entirely, Commands v3, OpMode framework (FTC-style), Telemetry + Tunable APIs replacing SmartDashboard/Shuffleboard, single `Gamepad` class. Removed HW support: relay, analog output, SPI + SPI IMUs, analog gyro, DMA, built-in accelerometer, digital glitch filter, interrupts, counter, ultrasonic, analog trigger, Nidec Brushless, Servo, Jaguar (https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/yearly-overview/yearly-changelog.html). CTRE `corvus` 26.3.0 already generates Arm/Elevator/Flywheel subsystems from JSON but explicitly "does not support generating Java mechanisms using WPILib Commands v3" (https://api.ctr-electronics.com/changelog.html).

patterns.name: Code generation instead of runtime abstraction (the strongest signal in the corpus)
patterns.whatItDoes: Emits plain, readable, editable WPILib/vendor subsystem source into the team's repo, rather than shipping a wrapper class the team must call into forever. Team owns the output; the generator is a one-shot accelerator, not a permanent dependency.
patterns.whereSeen: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/521681 (posts #75, #76); https://yamgen.com ; https://api.ctr-electronics.com/changelog.html (corvus CLI, added 2025-10-08, flywheel generator 26.3.0 2026-05-26); https://v6.docs.ctr-electronics.com/en/latest/docs/tuner/tuner-swerve/index.html (Tuner X Swerve + Elevator generators); https://yteam3211.github.io (FRC Catalyst Subsystem Generator, community-built)
patterns.libraryValue: DylanB (CSA): "YAMGen is the most useful part of the YASS stack in my opinion. The fact that it doesn't use the rest of YAMS is a strength, not a weakness. Most of our subsystems started off as YAMGen templates… I'd argue that the codegen route is far more useful than YAMS, and comes with fewer footguns." tekdemo reported the same for a sibling rookie team: "they used YAMGEN to create the boilerplate, copy-paste it into the project, and then edit it to wire things up… saved a lot of time. They're planning to repeat this workflow next year." Codegen simultaneously solves the debuggability objection (a CSA can read the generated file), the vendor-lock objection, and the year-over-year breaking-change objection — the generated code doesn't break when the generator does. CTRE is already doing this, so Rootstock should either differentiate on it or interop with it.
patterns.codeSketch: rootstock gen mechanism --type=arm --motor=TalonFX:13 --encoder=CANcoder:20 --out src/main/java/frc/robot/subsystems/Arm.java   # emits ~120 lines of plain WPILib+Phoenix6, no rootstock import

patterns.name: Config-over-code drivetrain (JSON/declarative, hardware-swappable)
patterns.whatItDoes: Entire swerve stack described by a config directory; changing motor vendor or module type is a data edit, not a code edit.
patterns.whereSeen: https://docs.yagsl.com/ ; https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/450844 (YAGSL v1 release thread, 767 posts); https://github.com/HuskieRobotics/3061-lib (multi-robot configs for practice bot vs comp bot vs mechanism test bed)
patterns.libraryValue: This is YAGSL's actual pitch and it demonstrably works — reported case of swapping NEOs to Krakens with ~4 lines of JSON. 3061-lib's variant (one codebase, several named robot configs) is the underrated half: it lets a small team keep a practice bot, a comp bot and a bare swerve test chassis on one branch, which is how you get software time before the comp bot exists. BUT see painPoint 'wall of knobs' — config-over-code only pays off if the config is structured to mirror the physical system and self-diagnoses.

patterns.name: Mechanism archetypes mapped to WPILib physics sim models
patterns.whatItDoes: Collapse every FRC subsystem to Arm/Pivot (position), Elevator/Linear (position, gravity FF), Flywheel/Roller (velocity or open loop), each with a real physics model so it simulates on day 1.
patterns.whereSeen: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/521681 posts #60, #62, #64 (Cole Hunt / ArchdukeTim taxonomy debate); https://yams.yamgen.com ; https://github.com/TomAs-1226/FrcCatalyst
patterns.libraryValue: Community converged on this taxonomy independently and it maps 1:1 onto WPILib's `SingleJointedArmSim`/`ElevatorSim`/`FlywheelSim`, which is what makes sim free. ArchdukeTim's refinement is the correct one: the distinguishing axis is *the controlled quantity* (position vs velocity vs open-loop), NOT the pivot geometry. Watch the gap: teams reported missing intake/indexer/roller and extendable-hopper archetypes in YAMS, so ship Roller and Winch/Telescope as first-class names even though they're degenerate cases.

patterns.name: IO-interface layer + deterministic log replay
patterns.whatItDoes: Subsystem logic depends on an `XIO` interface with `XIOInputs` structs; real/sim/replay implementations swap underneath; entire robot cycle replayable from a log in sim.
patterns.whereSeen: https://docs.advantagekit.org/getting-started/what-is-advantagekit/ ; https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/AdvantageKit ; https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/509227 ; 254-inspired generic IO structure discussed at https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/513448/11
patterns.libraryValue: 600+ teams in 2025, 200+ on the swerve templates — this is the closest thing FRC has to a de facto architecture. Karl Olson's point is the one to steal: "the fact that there is repetitive code for the autocomplete to pick up on should make you wonder why you are writing it multiple times… a generic structure heavily inspired by 254's… almost completely removed manual IO implementation for us and killed all of the subtle differences that we had when different team members wrote IO implementations." The AdvantageKit IO pattern's cost is boilerplate; that boilerplate is exactly what codegen should eliminate, not what a runtime wrapper should hide.

patterns.name: Sim-first workflow: code complete before the robot exists
patterns.whatItDoes: Full subsystem + command logic developed and unit-tested in WPILib sim (plus maple-sim for drivetrain/game-piece physics) during build weeks 1–4 when programmers have no hardware; the robot arrives only for gain tuning.
patterns.whereSeen: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/509817 ("Biding Time for Programmers", Jan 2026); https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/wpilib-tools/robot-simulation/introduction.html ; https://github.com/Shenzhen-Robotics-Alliance/maple-sim ; https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/523071 (Aug 2026, rookie team from Türkiye already sim-first)
patterns.libraryValue: httpmaster's workflow is the target UX verbatim: "I start coding for those using a combination of MapleSim and WPILib sim classes. By the time the bot is built, it is fully coded and ready for PID tuning." And from a YASS user: "my code can't be wrong because of YAMS because my team know 100% before we put code on the robot that the logic should work because we can simulate every functionality." For 2027 this stops being a nice-to-have: SystemCore hardware does not exist in team hands until KOP (Jan 2027), so sim is the ONLY development target for the entire 2026-27 offseason. WPILib's own caveat to respect: "Not all vendors will support this option, and code that uses their libraries may even crash when attempting to run simulation!"

patterns.name: Live tuning that behaves identically in sim and on hardware
patterns.whatItDoes: Every gain/setpoint exposed as a tunable with the same semantics whether the loop is running in sim or on the robot, so students can practice tuning without robot access and gains transfer.
patterns.whereSeen: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/521681/11 (nstrike: "This is why I built live tuning (that works the same in sim and in real life), its perfectly safe for students to learn how to tune everything without risk of breaking the robot"); https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/520826 post #12 (first feature request after the follower fix: "tunable numbers on the mechanism pid and motionmagic by default"); https://mantik.netlify.app/ /pid-simulation (browser PID trainer built precisely because "PID simulation/tuning was the most confusing part of the process")
patterns.libraryValue: Direct answer to 'tune without a robot.' CRITICAL 2027 constraint: WPILib is adding a first-party **Tunable** API alongside the new **Telemetry** API (Peter Johnson, https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/517572/14). Rootstock should adopt/extend those, not invent a competing tunables system — inventing one is exactly the kind of duplicate abstraction the community punished YASS for.

patterns.name: Escape hatch: accept and pass through the raw vendor config
patterns.whatItDoes: Any wrapper accepts a native vendor config object (e.g. `TalonFXConfiguration`) and merges it, so teams never hit a wall where the abstraction can't express what the hardware does.
patterns.whereSeen: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/521681 posts #63, #68 ; https://yagsl.gitbook.io (YAMS 'Passing a Vendor Config')
patterns.libraryValue: YASS *has* this feature and still lost users over it because it was buried: "Passing a vendor config into YAMS sounds like useful information that shouldn't be in a topic buried all the way on the bottom and near the end of said topic. honestly that should be on page 1 of the YAMS docs." Make the escape hatch a page-1, first-example feature. It directly defuses the #1 abandonment reason (SLAB-Mr.Thomas: libraries "may solve 90% or more of what you need but they become intractable if you try to force yourself into those libraries to tweak the last 5% or 10% that they don't provide. (As you noticed they tend to resist intrusion.)")

patterns.name: Named setpoint registry on the mechanism
patterns.whatItDoes: Positions registered by name at config time and driven by `goTo("HIGH")`, so the operator bindings and autos read in game language and the numbers live in one place.
patterns.libraryValue: Small but high-leverage for small teams: it removes the single most common last-minute-at-competition edit (retuning setpoints) from the code path and into a table a non-programmer can read.

patterns.name: Pre-match self-test / system check + persistent Alerts as the debugging surface
patterns.whatItDoes: One button runs a scripted health check of every device (CAN presence, firmware, encoder direction, limit switches, temperature) and reports plain-English pass/fail; runtime misconfiguration raises WPILib Alerts rather than silent misbehavior.
patterns.whereSeen: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/520826 post #31 (FrcCatalyst 'Pre match SystemCheck'); https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/521681 posts #11, #18, #29 (Alerts vs compile-time errors debate); https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/telemetry/persistent-alerts.html ; https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/505274 (254 CheesyCare + 694 PulseCrew field-failure lists: "Miswired CANcoders: Wrong CAN and encoder wiring were frequent, especially on swerve robots", "Controller Mapping & Binding Errors: Several teams couldn't drive because joysticks were inverted or mapped incorrectly")
patterns.libraryValue: The two largest CSA orgs' published field-failure lists are overwhelmingly config/wiring mismatches that a library can detect programmatically. kn4 explicitly wished for this: "I'm thinking about implementing code in the robot program that displays something similar to the driver station joysticks tab on a dashboard… it should be possible to use DriverStation.getJoystickName and automatically send an alert if a gamepad ended up in the wrong slot." Prefer compile-time where possible (Sam948: "compile-time issues would help, as the problem can be found before the driver is given the robot"; note WPILib 2026 already added "a javac plugin for detecting common error cases at compile time" and 2027 adds "compile-time checks for unsafe or incorrect coroutine usage").

patterns.name: Alliance/field-frame utilities and pose flipping
patterns.whatItDoes: First-class helpers for blue-origin vs alliance-relative poses, mirroring a point to the other alliance, field dimensions, and correct alliance handling in field-centric drive.
patterns.whereSeen: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500529 post #4 (Scott W, 4907); https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/505274 post #17 (a team that "hard coded the robot alliance each match until we had time to sort out the issue after the event")
patterns.libraryValue: Repeatedly requested from WPILib and repeatedly a source of on-field failures. Cheap to provide, high perceived value, no abstraction cost, zero controversy.

patterns.name: Shoot-on-the-fly / virtual-goal aiming as pure testable math
patterns.whatItDoes: Motion-compensated aiming solver with no hardware dependency so it can be unit tested and simulated.
patterns.whereSeen: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/520826 post #31 (Catalyst AimingSolver, "pure math with no hardware dependency, so you can unit test it"); 2026 REBUILT made turrets + accuracy the meta (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519847 posts #4, #16); https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/515752 ("Turret Undershooting while Shooting on the Fly")
patterns.libraryValue: Game-agnostic, high-value, and hardware-free — which means it's testable in CI and teachable without a robot. Also the correct architectural example for the whole library: separate the math (pure, tested) from the plumbing (thin, visible).

patterns.name: Declarative state machine — DO NOT BUILD, ADOPT
patterns.whatItDoes: Explicit states + transitions with full scheduler visibility, replacing opaque nested command groups.
patterns.whereSeen: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/520547 ("How to learn state-based programming", May 2026); https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/yearly-overview/yearly-changelog.html ("Add a declarative state machine API on top of commands v3"); https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/522893 post #6 (Karl Olson replying to FrcCatalyst's whole-robot state machine: "There is one in standard WPILib now.")
patterns.libraryValue: Sam Carlberg (WPILib) on why teams want it: "Part of the issue with v2 commands is that it's impossible to know what your command groups are doing; the command scheduler only knows which groups are running, but not what those groups are doing under the hood. v3 fixes it by making every command run in the scheduler and gives you full access to that information." A Rootstock state machine in 2027 would be an immediate, publicly-called-out duplication of core WPILib.

painPoints.problem: Swerve bring-up is the single largest consumer of small-team software time, and the failures are almost never conceptual — they're direction/offset/units/CAN-ID mismatches.
painPoints.evidence: A single Chief Delphi search returns ~25 distinct 2025-26 threads that are literally 'YAGSL <specific failure>': https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/505012 (motors turning randomly, 45 posts), /t/507058 (field not oriented, 33p), /t/510584 (need help with YAGSL for 2026, 29p), /t/514521 (turning at max speed all the time), /t/514414 (constant spinning), /t/513840 (starting orientation), /t/511769 (gyro config), /t/514232 (encoder error), /t/516937 ("sticky" driving), /t/522068 (input lag). guineawheek: "I worry about the team I saw at both our 2025 regionals that tried to run YAGSL but despite the best efforts of several CSAs and local mentors working with them for the entirety of both events were never able to drive their swerve straight…which meant they spent most of their matches getting in the way of all their partners" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/521681/43). His list of the actually-hard questions: "How do absolute encoders interface with said starting position? …What are the units of measurement for the closed-loop PID? Where are they measured from? How do you deal with a gear ratio difference between your external encoder and your motor? What direction is positive? What if your encoder and motor spin in opposite directions? How do you tell which direction is positive when testing?"
painPoints.libraryFix: Do not ship 'a swerve library.' Ship a *guided bring-up procedure* that answers guineawheek's list empirically: an interactive wizard/CLI that, one module at a time, spins the motor and asks the user what they observed, derives inverts/offsets/units from the answers, and writes the config. Emit a signed 'bring-up report' the team can hand a CSA. Make every derived quantity displayed with units and a direction convention diagram. This is the highest-ROI feature in the entire space and nobody has shipped it — YAGSL/CTRE generators configure, they don't *verify*.

painPoints.problem: 'Wall of knobs' config: when something is wrong, neither a student nor a visiting CSA can bisect which knob is misconfigured, or whether it's user error / library bug / vendor bug / version regression.
painPoints.evidence: guineawheek, opening the 2026 YASS feedback thread with a screenshot of a YAMS config block: "my first thought is 'if something is wrong, how do you even figure out which knob is misconfigured?' …Was an option that needed to be specified missing? Is there one that shouldn't be there? Is it a bug in the library? A regression between versions? …Personally, I have a crippling fear of code that I have no inkling how to fix if something goes wrong" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/521681/2). DAflamingFOX: "how / where in the world would I even begin to start looking if I had a problem? How do I know if it's a user issue…, a YASS issue, a vendor issue, etc." (#4). joel truher's diagnosis is the constructive one: "the configuration model seems much 'flatter' than the real world. Everything is in one place, which is convenient, but doesn't reveal anything about the attached real-world system… maybe your concern about knowing which knob to turn can be addressed by making the wall of knobs more inescapably structured" (#6).
painPoints.libraryFix: Structure config to mirror physical topology, not a flat builder chain: motor → gearbox → sensor → mechanism, each a nested object that names the real part. Every config object gets a `describe()` that prints the derived physical model ("3.2 rotations of the motor = 1 inch of travel; positive = up; absolute encoder reads 0.31 at hard stop"). Ship a `rootstock doctor` that diffs live device state against the config and reports the *first* mismatch in plain English with the config line number. Version-stamp everything in telemetry so 'regression between versions' is answerable from a log.

painPoints.problem: A single monolithic motor-controller abstraction across vendors hides that on-motor-controller loops and on-controller (RIO/SystemCore) loops behave completely differently — same API, wildly different control behavior.
painPoints.evidence: Oblarg (WPILib maintainer): "it attempts to paper over fundamental differences in capability with identical APIs, where a small change in config metadata can/will precipitate a massive change in mechanism behavior. Loops running on the RIO and loops running on peripheral controllers are really not comparable… things that are distant performance-wise should be distant in terms of code structure. It is fine to abstract out shared datatypes… but it is extremely unwise to wrap the entire thing in a shared monolithic API" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/521681/7, /42). Even the YASS author concedes the failure mode: "when a team has tuned the PID/FF for the motor controller, then they attempt to use a motion profile that switches the entire control loop to the SystemCore… they should find out what happened" (#15). Single-vendor teams reject it outright: "it doesn't solve the problem of smc overabstracting our $200 krakens just so they can fit the lowest common denominator, making it inherently worse than just using the official ctre api" (#61); "The fact that it is just abstracting what Krakens do natively and I see no point in putting CTRE native functions into an extra wrapper… We really wanted to use it, but gave up cause it was too overcomplicated" (#20).
painPoints.libraryFix: Share *config data types* (feedforward gains, gear ratios, soft limits, current limits) across vendors; do NOT share the control-execution API. Give on-motor closed loop and on-controller closed loop separate, differently-named entry points so the choice is visible in the code and in the diff. Consider scoping v1 to one vendor family (FrcCatalyst's Phoenix-6-only scope drew explicit praise: "I really like the ctre focus because I think it makes the underlying code really easy to understand and simplifies everything", https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/520826/4) and expanding only where the shared shape is genuinely identical.

painPoints.problem: Documentation rot is the fastest abandonment trigger — examples that don't compile against current API, or that are subtly wrong.
painPoints.evidence: tekdemo, evaluating YAMS post-season by deliberately behaving like a freshman: "several of the examples on the site didn't work with the actual code. Several APIs had changed (the gear reduction is the one I recall)… Even once getting it working, the sim mechanism it represented simply didn't work at all… If that had hit us mid-season when looking at YAMS, we'd just immediately drop it. The value add is not worth potentially misleading or wrong documentation" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/521681/45). ArchdukeTim found a physics error in the docs: YAMS said arms are at 0° parallel to ground "this way the feedforward calculations can be done with the sin of the angle" — "This statement is simply incorrect. cos should be used… So now I don't even know if I can trust this library to accurately control my mechanism" (#66). The maintainer's reply reveals the mechanism: "Documentation is really difficult to get right and keep up to date. So i had used AI to try to eleviate some of this" and "Keep in mind i do not update the documentation at the same time as the program" (#67, #71) — which drew: "the use of AI, making such a simple mistake, and not getting caught by anyone until now is concerning to me" (#70).
painPoints.libraryFix: Every doc example must be a compiled, executed, asserted test — extract snippets from real test files at build time, never hand-write code in prose. CI fails if a snippet doesn't compile against the pinned WPILib/vendor version. Version-pin the docs site to the release. Any AI-assisted prose must be gated behind a human physics/API review; a single wrong sin/cos costs more trust than ten missing pages. Ship a discoverable feature index on the landing page (ArchdukeTim's complaint: "I just want to find out what the overall features of YAMS are, and what mechanisms it supports, to decide if it fits my use case or not" — instead 'Getting Started' dumped him into an arm tutorial).

painPoints.problem: Programmers get no robot for the first 4+ weeks of build, and even after that, hands-on time is rationed against driver practice.
painPoints.evidence: "This is my first build season where I actually get to contribute to the robot code, but I do am worried that there will be much to do for the first half of the season besides the occasional swerve test and formatting some boilerplate code" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/509817). guineawheek on why this matters: "debugging speed is incredibly important in FRC; a program where most teams give relatively little hands-on time to programmers. Every hour spent debugging is an hour you're not spending doing driver practice" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/521681/43). A ~10-student team that finished top-tier: "Plan to finish the bot early mechanically: We had the bot driving by the end of build week 4. This let us spend several weeks fine-tuning software… to place coral fast this year you basically needed auto-align" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/506421/17). Time budgets from teams that qualify for DCMP/CMP: 14–22 hours/week of *whole-team* meeting time in build season (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/415621 posts #2, #12, #13); a minimal-viable competitive schedule was sketched at 6 hours/week total with 4 students, with programming explicitly deferred to weeks 6–7 (#8).
painPoints.libraryFix: Make 'zero-hardware' a supported, documented, first-class mode, not an afterthought: `./gradlew simulateJava` must give a working robot with physics, a dashboard layout, keyboard/gamepad control and tunables on the first run of a fresh project. Ship a headless sim harness for CI so autos and state machines are regression-tested without a robot. Budget the on-robot workflow to <30 minutes: guided swerve bring-up, then characterization, then gains — and make gains transfer from sim as a starting point rather than starting from zero.

painPoints.problem: The one or two students who understand the codebase graduate, and the knowledge (sometimes the code itself) leaves with them.
painPoints.evidence: "At the start of this off-season, our only two experienced programmers — the ones who handled complex mechanisms like swerve drive and state machines — left the team. Unfortunately, they also deleted the working code before leaving, so we lost everything… They managed to find an early-season backup, but even that version didn't have the swerve drive fully implemented" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/504585). "it is our first year in FRC as programmers. We can't really figure it out trough the documents and stuff beacuse we don't exactly know how to get everything together… we are the only programmers plus we can't let the team down" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/515511). A rookie team with strong mechanical/business: "Programming is still where we have the most to grow. We've got 2–3 students who can build a full robot program (without vision), but we're still trying to figure out how to get the rest of our programmers to that level. Since we're a rookie team, we don't really have a solid training roadmap yet" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/523071). bly: "so much of FRC software is tribal knowledge or obscure info buried deep in old cd threads" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/506826/17).
painPoints.libraryFix: Optimize for the *second* year, not the first. Config should be the durable artifact (checked in, human-readable, diffable) so a new student can read the robot's physical description without reading control code. Generated code should carry provenance comments ("generated by rootstock gen v27.1.0 from config/arm.json — regenerate with …"). Ship a repo scaffold that includes the boring survival infrastructure small teams skip: git remote, CI, a CHANGELOG of config edits, and a one-page ROBOT.md that the generator keeps current. Consider an explicit 'explain mode' that prints the derived control math so a student can learn from their own robot's config.

painPoints.problem: Rookie programmers don't fail at control theory — they fail at Java OOP and the periodic/callback execution model, which every template silently assumes.
painPoints.evidence: guineawheek: "I worry about the kids who might have a decent grasp on the basics of if statements and for loops and System.out.println but not so much Java classes and objects, or how to write code in a system that's always calling some sort of periodic function. That's the sorta stuff that FRC programming tends to not bridge well" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/521681/43). martinma's list of what's actually missing from FRC curricula: "Passing function as data / Method reference / Lambda expression… / Runtime polymorphism / Dependency injection / Instance factory method / Supplier / Command design pattern… WPIlib documentation really tries to teach you everything mixed together at once which can be overwhelming" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/522085/2). Tom Line: "Every year, 25% of the programmers are new. Most code examples show the semantics, but doesn't give you an idea of where it would be appropriate to put it… Should it normal be in robot.java? RobotContainer? A subsystem? The constructor? Periodic?" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500529/14). tekdemo on why YAMS didn't fit his sibling rookie team: "What YAMS asks of that for the initial SmartMotorController setup is above what they can quickly learn early on. But similarly, if we start learning the fundamentals with our Rev controllers, and then try to move to YAMS we have to basically start over… So we effectively just… don't have a place to insert YAMs into our workflow" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/521681/38).
painPoints.libraryFix: Design an explicit *on-ramp gradient* so the library can be adopted mid-learning-curve rather than all-or-nothing: Level 0 = make a motor spin with vendor API (library not involved); Level 1 = wrap that existing, already-configured vendor object (`Rootstock.adopt(existingTalonFX)`) to gain sim + telemetry + tunables with zero re-learning; Level 2 = full builder/codegen. tekdemo literally described the workflow he wanted and couldn't get. Also state, per file, where the code belongs — generated files land in the right place automatically, which sidesteps Tom Line's problem entirely.

painPoints.problem: Layers of abstraction are perceived as pedagogically hostile — and the argument is loud, public, and will be aimed at any new library.
painPoints.evidence: DAflamingFOX: "What I see is the challenging lessons of learning the advanced control systems being taken away from the students, and instead giving them a handful of vague and obscure dials and knobs to control various black boxes" and "you can't just give someone a calculator and say you've taught them calculus" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/521681/4, /21). Adam Gaddis: "the sheer amount of abstractions being layered on top of abstractions worries me personally. This take isn't reserved only for YASS; while I find AKit to be neat I also know that it is yet another unnecessary abstraction… why not just expand the collection of examples within WPILib itself?" (#47). Oblarg on ProfiledPIDController-style convenience: "If you are unwilling/unable to pass a few doubles around, then you are going to have a bad time. An API that makes it appear more friendly than it is will not help you - it will just lie to you. Checking the logs for the intermediate data becomes much harder when you have to do so through several layers of abstraction that do nothing but hide the plumbing" (#17). Counterweight worth citing back: Jared Russell — "Nothing screams '100% student-written' quite like calling a single .set() method that invokes a 50,000-line, mentor-built, closed-source vendor dependency to do all the actual math… Let's not pretend we aren't all heavily relying on code we didn't write!" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/520752/18).
painPoints.libraryFix: Pick the defensible position explicitly and state it in the README: Rootstock generates and instruments code students can read, rather than hiding it. Every abstraction must make the intermediate signals *more* visible in logs, not less (log setpoint, measurement, error, FF term, FB term, applied output for every loop, automatically). Publish a 'what this replaces' page showing the generated/hidden code side-by-side with raw WPILib. Ship teaching material as a deliverable, not a footnote (Mantik and frcsoftware.org exist precisely because this gap is unfilled: https://mantik.netlify.app/ , https://github.com/frcsoftware/frcsoftware.org).

painPoints.problem: Loop overruns and CPU cost get attributed to the library's structure, fairly or not — and small teams have no way to tell.
painPoints.evidence: "I can definitely attest to the loop overruns issue when using YAMS" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/521681/8). "For us, YAMS caused more problems than it solved. The structure of it created a crazy amount of loop overruns, forcing us to spend many hours trying to get this under control. We ended up not using any logging or telemetry at all" (#74). "we had some trouble debugging quickly and we also had a lot of loop overruns" using the AdvantageKit CTRE swerve template (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/520547/1). Also https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/516167 (Loop Overruns with Advantage Kit), /t/517228 ("nearly constant event loop overruns… CPU on the Rio is running around 80-90%"), /t/513431 ("Advantage Kit Swerve Template is sluggish"). Sam Carlberg's correction is important: "Loop overruns are completely unrelated to how your code is structured. Overruns are caused by garbage collection… and long-running or inefficient algorithms" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/520547/9).
painPoints.libraryFix: Ship per-subsystem timing and allocation telemetry ON by default with a budget, so blame is attributable in one glance rather than by bisection. Make telemetry volume a tiered config (off / minimal / full) so a team under CPU pressure disables logging by config rather than by deleting it. Set allocation-free hot paths as an explicit, tested invariant (JMH or a simple allocation counter in CI). SystemCore's Cortex-A76 relieves but does not eliminate this.

painPoints.problem: LLMs are now a primary onboarding tool for small teams, and they hallucinate badly against FRC's fast-moving APIs — which will get worse at the 2027 package rename.
painPoints.evidence: "AI would also recommend use of deprecated classes from former versions of wpilib… When my students attempted to use AI to troubleshoot, I noticed it would give the wrong solution about 80% of the time" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/520752/10). "certain specific AI models in particular experience a lot of hallucinations with WPILIB. This is natural because we see some major changes in the libraries every year" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/513448/10). "I asked GPT-5-mini to write tank drive code as a quick test, and it wrote a weird hybrid of time-based code and modern command-based code using outdated APIs" (#6). "half of our DS side control system was written by a vibe coder and failed completely first time we tried to use it. It had to be rewritten from scratch… the evening of day 1 of comp" (#12). And the failure mode that matters at an event: "how fast the vibe coded robot strategy breaks down when you're queuing and a mechanism isn't working and no one can figure out why and the LLM is still generating a response" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/520752/13).
painPoints.libraryFix: Treat LLMs as a first-class consumer of the docs: publish `llms.txt` and `.md` mirrors of every docs page (YAGSL already does this: https://docs.yagsl.com/llms.txt), keep a machine-readable API index per version, and make error messages self-describing enough that pasting one into a chat yields the right fix. Keep the public API surface small and *stable across the 2027 rename* — the more the library's own API churns, the more it inherits WPILib's hallucination problem.

painPoints.problem: Bus factor and abandonment risk: the batteries-included libraries in this space are one-to-few-person projects, and teams know it.
painPoints.evidence: YASS docs are written by essentially one person: "Time is a thing. A thing that i lack when writing docs pages. It took me 1 week to write a single page on avg before AI for ex. This is not my day job and takes away from time with my family too" and "I am normally the only one who works on docs" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/521681/71). FrcCatalyst: 11 GitHub stars, essentially one student author, README says "Made by an FRC team for FRC teams" (https://github.com/TomAs-1226/FrcCatalyst); community first reaction was "there are already so many other solutions out there, and the code behind this seem sketchy at best" and an immediate "How much (if any) was AI written?" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/522893 posts #2, #5). Hardware-side precedent for the risk: Redux Robotics' motor controllers were shelved, taking their vendor library with them ("the vendor library for Redux's [unfortunately deceased] motor controllers… it's a shame that they're all shelved", https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/521681/40 ; https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/506991). DAflamingFOX's stability question is the one every mentor will ask: "With WPILib, we have guarantees that their APIs are locked for a season… How does YASS, with many different dependencies & abstraction layers… guarantee stability for teams?" (#4).
painPoints.libraryFix: Publish an explicit support contract on page 1: API frozen for the season after kickoff; semver; a documented deprecation window; a public test matrix of vendor/WPILib versions actually validated. Prefer source-available templates + codegen over an opaque vendordep so the library's death is survivable (teams keep working generated code). Name >1 maintainer, publish CI status and test count. Distribute a fully self-contained project zip AND a vendordep, and mirror releases.

painPoints.problem: Onboarding friction in *distribution* kills adoption before the library is even evaluated.
painPoints.evidence: AdvantageKit 2026 template distribution confusion: "I don't get how the template projects work… When I look in the repository I see 'template_projects' and inside that then 'sources', 'template' and more. What am I supposed to download as the project?" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/509227/6). Then a formatter/`wpilib_preferences.json` interaction broke project detection for multiple users: "Cannot Build Robot Code since this is not a WPILib project" / "it randomly works when I restart vs code sometimes and then will go back to not being a wpilib project again" (#12, #15, #16, #17). Also YASS docs-site navigation complaints (#21) and dead links on launch day (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/506826/7). Support-channel exclusion is real too: a Turkish team could not use the Discord-only support path — "I do have Discord but currently in our country it is banned" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/515511/18).
painPoints.libraryFix: One command, one artifact: a single downloadable zip per template that opens, builds, deploys and simulates with zero edits, plus a `rootstock init` CLI. Smoke-test the shipped zip in CI on Windows/macOS/Linux (the macOS-default-unzip case is exactly what broke AdvantageKit). Keep all documentation on a public web page reachable without an account; treat Discord as supplementary, and keep a Chief Delphi thread and GitHub Discussions as the canonical, publicly-searchable support surface.

painPoints.problem: Vision is the area small teams self-report as weakest, and it is the hardest thing to simulate.
painPoints.evidence: Rookie team's own assessment: "vision and building a structured programming development process are still our weakest areas… once those ideas start relying on vision, we quickly hit a wall because that's the area we're least confident in" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/523071). aopalka: "Vision is another great 'next' level topic and one that is hard to simulate though. You will need some sort of test bed for that in my experience to really do it effectively" (same thread, #9). WPILib docs feedback: "The Vision documentation could now be considered the bad. It appears most teams use LL or PV and rarely any of the WPILib AprilTag classes. It's hard to find the information we need among the preponderance of information that is not needed" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500529/12). YALL (the Limelight wrapper) shipped without simulation support and had a multi-camera bug: "YALL had a bug that prevented it from accepting more than one camera, resulting in another late-night session" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/521681/74). Counterpoint on what works: PhotonVision "has great native support" for simulation (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/523071/5).
painPoints.libraryFix: Lean on PhotonVision's simulator rather than wrapping vendors; ship a vision template whose *only* job is correct pose-estimation plumbing (camera-to-robot transforms, per-measurement standard deviations, ambiguity/latency rejection, multi-camera fusion) with those rejection rules exposed as logged, tunable, testable values. Provide a recorded-log replay path so vision tuning happens off-robot. Do not attempt a unified LL/PV abstraction — gold856's point that the two are 'completely different code-wise, up until you input the data into a SwerveDrivePoseEstimator' defines exactly where the shared surface begins.

painPoints.problem: Small teams that succeed do so by doing fewer things well — a maximalist library is a strategic mismatch for its own audience.
painPoints.evidence: "Intentionally build less robot than you're capable of" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/506421/6). "Pick a couple things (2-5), and do them well… Do fewer things, but practice them" (#19). "Limit custom machined parts / Choose simple mechanisms / Don't do everything" (#18). "Be sure to design and build within your means. Nothing will sink a season faster than trying to bite off more than you can chew" (#5). Yet the feature-list arms race is the norm: FrcCatalyst v1 advertises 10 mechanism types + swerve + vision + LEDs + reactive autonomy + a utility-based Strategist + a teleop co-pilot + whole-robot state machine (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/520826/31), and the very next season CTRE, WPILib and YASS all shipped overlapping versions of the same primitives.
painPoints.libraryFix: Scope v1 ruthlessly and say no in the README. Highest-value, least-contested surface for a small team: (1) guided swerve bring-up + verification, (2) sim-first mechanism scaffolding via codegen, (3) tuning workflow that works in sim and transfers, (4) pre-match self-test + plain-English alerts, (5) alliance/pose utilities. Explicitly defer: state machines (WPILib 2027 ships one), logging/replay (AdvantageKit), pathing (PathPlanner/Choreo), dashboards (Elastic/AdvantageScope), vision processing (PV/LL).

constraints: HARD, NON-NEGOTIABLE: target WPILib 2027 / SystemCore, not 2026. Peter Johnson (WPILib): "There will be no support for the RoboRIO in the 2027 version of WPILib, and the library changes are significant enough that it will not be possible to have the same code target both the 2026 and 2027 libraries." (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/517572/14). Java packages move `edu.wpi.first` → `org.wpilib`, C++ `frc::` → `wpi::`; Java 25 / C++23; NetworkTables v3 support removed entirely. (https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/yearly-overview/yearly-changelog.html). A Rootstock written against 2026 is throwaway work.

Commands v3 is the 2027 command framework and is coroutine-based (`coroutine.yield()` inside loops, `coroutine.fork()`); WPILib is adding "compile-time checks for unsafe or incorrect coroutine usage". Teams can only import CommandsV2 OR CommandsV3 as a vendordep, and "any templates you may use may dictate which version you are stuck using" (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/523071/9). Rootstock must pick, state it loudly, and ideally keep its mechanism/math layer command-framework-agnostic so it isn't stranded. Note CTRE's corvus explicitly "does not support generating Java mechanisms using WPILib Commands v3" as of 26.x — an opening, and a warning about how much work v3 support is.

Do NOT reimplement things WPILib 2027 now ships: a declarative state machine API on commands v3; the Telemetry API (SmartDashboard's replacement); the Tunable API; persistent Alerts; Epilogue `@Logged` annotation logging; a javac plugin for compile-time error detection; unit types. Karl Olson already publicly answered a competing library's 'whole-robot state machine' feature with "There is one in standard WPILib now." (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/522893/6).

Removed in 2027 and unavailable to build on: Shuffleboard, SmartDashboard, PathWeaver, RobotBuilder, NetworkTables v3. Removed SystemCore hardware capabilities: relay, analog output, SPI and SPI IMUs, analog gyro, DMA, built-in accelerometer, digital glitch filter, interrupts, counter, ultrasonic, analog trigger, Nidec Brushless, Servo, Jaguar. Any config schema assuming these is dead on arrival.

No team has SystemCore hardware and probably will not before the 2027 KOP (~January 2027). Expected sequence per WPILib's Peter Johnson: extra units purchasable fall 2026 "but will not have software ready to go to actually use it on a robot"; a fall 2026 FRC beta; SystemCore in every team's 2027 KOP; roboRIO not legal in 2027 (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/517572 posts #7, #9). CONSEQUENCE: simulation is the only viable development and demo target for Rootstock for the entire remaining offseason, and 'works in sim' must be the library's primary proof of correctness. Teams building SystemCore clones from Raspberry Pi + hats exist (https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/520408, Bobcat SystemClone in https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/522511) — worth supporting as a test target.

Debuggability by a stranger is a functional requirement, not a nicety. A CSA who has never seen Rootstock must be able to diagnose a robot at an event without reading the library source. Design test: can someone answer guineawheek's questions — "Was an option that needed to be specified missing? Is there one that shouldn't be there? Is it a bug in the library? A regression between versions?" — from the dashboard and the DS log alone? If not, the design fails.

Never wrap a vendor API monolithically without a page-1 escape hatch. Shared *config data* across vendors is acceptable; a shared *control-execution* API across on-motor and on-controller loops is the specific mistake the community rejected. If in doubt, scope v1 to one vendor family — narrow scope was explicitly praised, breadth explicitly punished.

Documentation correctness is a release blocker. Every code example must be compiled and executed in CI against the pinned WPILib + vendor versions. AI-generated docs shipped a wrong feedforward trig identity that destroyed a reviewer's trust in the whole library in one post; assume this failure mode is fatal, not cosmetic.

Season-locked API stability. Mentors explicitly compare third-party libs unfavourably to WPILib's per-season API freeze. Commit publicly to: no breaking changes between kickoff and championship; semver; a written deprecation window; a published matrix of vendor/WPILib versions actually tested.

Support and distribution must not be Discord-only or account-gated. Discord is blocked in at least one active FRC country (Türkiye). Canonical support surface should be a public, search-indexed Chief Delphi thread + GitHub Issues/Discussions, with docs readable without login and mirrored as markdown/`llms.txt` for LLM consumption.

Must survive its own maintainer. Prefer generated, team-owned source over an opaque compiled vendordep wherever feasible, so that if Rootstock is abandoned, teams keep a working robot. Ship >1 named maintainer, public CI, and a test count. The Redux vendor-library shelving is the cautionary precedent teams already cite.

Java first. ~90% of FRC teams use Java and the Java ecosystem is the reason help is available at events ("in case you run into a issue in your very first event ever… it makes it so much easier for other teams to help you with your code because most teams use Java", https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/509064/22). RobotPy/Kotlin exist but are not the target for v1.

Performance budget: telemetry and abstraction must be tiered/disable-able by config, with per-subsystem timing exposed by default. Loop overruns were attributed to competing libraries repeatedly in 2026, and one team's response was to disable logging and telemetry entirely — a library whose observability is the first thing dropped under pressure has failed at its main job.

Assume the audience is 1–3 students with a partial grasp of Java OOP and no grasp of the periodic execution model, ~14–22 hrs/week of shared team time in build season (often far less), no dedicated programming mentor, and no robot until week 4+. Any workflow step that requires the robot, requires a mentor, or requires reading library source is a step most of the target audience will not complete.
